name: Assegno Unico Universale - SIA Project 24 25
description:
The system supports the online management of applications for the Italian
    Assegno Unico Universale (AUU), a financial benefit provided by INPS to
    families with dependent children. The considered scenario focuses exclusively
    on applications submitted directly by interested users through the INPS website,
    excluding applications submitted by delegated patronage institutions, mobile
    applications, and call-center interactions.

    An authenticated applicant can submit an AUU application as a parent,
    foster parent, or legal guardian of a child. During the first phase of the
    application, the applicant provides information about each dependent child,
    including the child's fiscal code, dependency status, disability status and,
    when applicable, disability level. Depending on the applicant type, additional
    information concerning family composition, exclusive custody, the other
    parent's fiscal code, and the requested allowance distribution between parents
    must also be provided.

    When a child's fiscal code is entered, the system verifies it in real time.
    If the child is already associated with another active application, the
    application flow is blocked and an explanatory warning is shown. The applicant
    may also specify adult dependent children who do not directly qualify for AUU
    but contribute to determining household composition. Duplicate fiscal codes for
    adult children are detected and reported.

    The amount of the allowance depends on the applicant's economic situation.
    If INPS does not already possess a valid ISEE when the application is submitted,
    the minimum allowance established by regulation is used. If a valid ISEE becomes
    available later, INPS automatically recalculates the allowance without requiring
    the applicant to modify the application.

    In the payment phase, the applicant specifies the payment method. If the
    allowance is to be divided equally between both parents, the payment information
    of the other parent must also be provided. Supported payment methods include
    credit to a SEPA IBAN account owned by the beneficiary, domiciled payment at a
    post office, and credit to an eligible prepaid card.

    Before submitting the application, the applicant must read and accept the
    declarations of responsibility and the GDPR privacy notice. The system then
    presents a summary of the entered information so that it can be reviewed.
    If validation errors are detected, the application is not submitted and the
    applicant must correct the erroneous information. If validation succeeds, the
    application is submitted and a receipt can be downloaded.

    An application may be interrupted without saving or saved as a draft before
    submission. A saved draft can later be consulted and completed. When resuming
    a draft, the applicant may either continue from the previously saved information
    or discard it and restart the application from the beginning.

    Once submitted, the application is evaluated by authorized INPS staff.
    The application may be accepted, rejected because the applicant is not entitled
    to the benefit, or suspended when additional documentation is required.
    The applicant is notified of the outcome. An accepted application remains valid
    for twelve months and the corresponding allowance is paid automatically every
    month.

    When an application is suspended, the INPS operator specifies which additional
    documents are required. The applicant can consult the application, upload the
    requested attachments, reconfirm the application data, and again accept the
    responsibility declarations and privacy notice.

    The system also allows an application originally submitted by one parent to be
    completed by the other parent. The other parent can consult the application and
    confirm or modify the proposed allowance distribution. If the applicant requested
    the entire allowance, the other parent may accept the 100 percent allocation or
    request a 50 percent distribution. When payment to the other parent is required,
    that parent provides their own payment information.

    Applicants can also add one or more children to an existing application.
    Each new child's fiscal code is checked in real time to ensure that the child
    is not already associated with another active application. After adding the
    child, existing payment and declaration data can be confirmed or modified.

    Finally, the system provides supporting functions that allow citizens to consult
    previously submitted applications, consult general information about the
    Assegno Unico Universale, and simulate the expected monthly allowance amount.

highLevelGoals: To successfully submit a new application for the Assegno Unico Universale (AUU) benefit, providing all necessary personal and child-related information.
To save an incomplete application as a draft and later resume or discard it, allowing for flexible completion of the application process.
To provide and manage the preferred method and details for receiving the AUU allowance.
To track the progress and outcome (accepted, rejected, suspended) of submitted AUU applications.

To consult general information about the AUU benefit and simulate potential allowance amounts.

To obtain a downloadable receipt as confirmation of successful application submission.

To ensure the approved AUU allowance is automatically disbursed to beneficiaries on a monthly basis for the duration of the application's validity.

The system must check if a submitted dependent fiscal code already exists among other dependents within the Applicant's current application. This could be implemented via an API call like GET /api/applications/{applicationId}/dependents/check-uniqueness?code={fiscalCode}.

The system must verify that a submitted dependent fiscal code is not already associated with an active, approved application by any other applicant in the entire system. This could be implemented via an API call like GET /api/dependents/check-global-uniqueness?code={fiscalCode}.

The system must query an external authoritative registry (e.g., national tax agency, civil registry) to fetch official demographic and status details for a validated dependent fiscal code. This could be implemented via an API call like GET /api/external-registry/dependent-details?fiscalCode={fiscalCode}.

The system must persist the successfully validated and enriched dependent fiscal code and associated official data into the Applicant's application record. This could be implemented via an API call like POST /api/applications/{applicationId}/dependents with the dependent data.

The system must provide clear and specific feedback to the Applicant, indicating success or detailing any validation errors (e.g., invalid format, duplicate within application, globally duplicate). This feedback would be part of the response from an API call like POST /api/applications/{applicationId}/dependents.

The system must enable the Applicant to select a preferred payment method (e.g., bank transfer, postal order) and capture the required payment details (e.g., IBAN, account holder name). This could be implemented via an API call like PUT /api/applications/{applicationId}/payment-method.

INPS Staff retrieves and reviews the outcome of an automatically triggered AUU allowance recalculation for a specific applicant, including the proposed new amount.
INPS Staff explicitly triggers the system to recalculate the AUU allowance for an applicant, overriding or re-running an automatic process if needed.
INPS Staff reviews the proposed new AUU allowance amount (resulting from an automatic or manual recalculation) and explicitly approves its update to the applicant's official record.
INPS Staff queries and views the detailed audit trail of an AUU allowance adjustment for a specific applicant, including old/new values, triggers (automatic/manual), and timestamps.
INPS Staff accesses and examines the current set of AUU allowance calculation rules and parameters used by the system for automatic adjustments.
INPS Staff reviews the content of an automated notification generated for an allowance adjustment for a specific applicant before or after its dispatch.

Applicant sends a request to the system to upload a specific supporting document file for their application.

Applicant sends a request to the system to select or modify their preferred payment method for receiving the AUU allowance.

The system shall allow an authenticated applicant to retrieve and continue editing a previously saved AUU application draft.
The system shall validate the entered child fiscal code against the national registry in real-time and display a warning if it is already linked to another active application.
The system shall allow an authenticated applicant to input and update details for each child associated with the AUU application.
The system shall allow an authenticated applicant to input and update family composition details relevant to the AUU application.
The system shall record the applicant's explicit acceptance of the responsibility declarations required for the AUU application submission.
The system shall record the applicant's explicit acceptance of the GDPR privacy notice.

The system shall allow an authenticated applicant to add details for a new child to an already submitted and active AUU application.
The system shall allow an authenticated applicant to view the status and details of their submitted AUU applications.
The system shall provide a tool for an authenticated applicant to simulate the potential AUU allowance amount based on entered family and income data.
The system shall allow INPS staff to access and review all submitted application details and supporting documentation for evaluation.

baselineCritiques.highLevelGoals: The list captures most of the functional intentions described, but there are a few issues. The goals “Automatically Adjust Allowance Based on ISEE” and “Ensure Timely Allowance Disbursement” describe system‑driven behavior rather than an explicit user‑oriented purpose; they belong to low‑level/technical goals and are incorrectly assigned to INPS staff. Additionally, the “Process and Decide on AUU Applications” goal could be split to explicitly include “Notify applicant of decision” which is only implied elsewhere. Overall the set is fairly complete, but the mis‑placement of automatic system actions lowers the score.
baselineCritiques.lowLevelGoals:
[Applicant -> Submit AUU Application] The low‑level goals are largely well‑aligned with the described user actions and are all functional. They cover initiating, drafting, editing, validating, and submitting an application, as well as handling second‑parent participation, document upload, payment details, and simulation. However, the set omits a key applicant action described in the specification: after the INPS staff evaluate the application, the applicant must be able to view the outcome (accepted, rejected, or suspended) and any associated decision document or notification. Adding low‑level goals such as “The system shall allow the Applicant to view the current status and decision of a submitted application” and “The system shall allow the Applicant to download the decision letter or notification” would make the list complete.

[Applicant -> Manage Application Drafts] The low‑level goals are all functional, each describes a single action the Applicant can perform on application drafts, and they map cleanly to the sole high‑level goal “Manage Application Drafts”. There are no non‑functional statements, contradictions, or missing actions for the draft‑management scope (create, update, list, load, delete). The set is complete for the defined high‑level goal.

[Applicant -> Manage AUU Allowance Payment Setup] The low‑level goal set is far from complete and is incorrectly structured. All goals are linked to a single high‑level goal (“Manage AUU Allowance Payment Setup”) even though many of them belong to other strategic objectives such as “Create and Manage AUU Application”, “Handle Supporting Documents”, “View Application Status”, “Simulate Allowance”, and “Co‑parent Collaboration”. Important functional actions described in the system narrative are missing, e.g.:

* Real‑time fiscal‑code validation that blocks duplicate active applications.  
* Adding adult dependent children and detecting duplicate adult fiscal codes.  
* Automatic recalculation of the allowance when a valid ISEE becomes available.  
* Receiving outcome notifications (accepted, rejected, suspended) and viewing the decision.  
* Uploading additional documents after a suspension and resubmitting.  
* Co‑parent actions: consulting the partner’s application, confirming/modifying allowance distribution, providing their own payment details, and accepting a 50 % split when the other parent requested 100 %.  
* Discarding a draft and restarting the application from scratch.  
* Consulting general information about AUU and running an allowance simulation.  

Conversely, the current list contains many goals that are unrelated to payment setup (e.g., “InitiateNewAUUApplication”, “AddChildDataToApplication”, “RequestAllowanceSimulation”) and therefore should be associated with appropriate high‑level goals.  

To improve the model you should:

1. Define additional high‑level goals that reflect the major business concerns (application creation, validation, draft management, outcome handling, co‑parent collaboration, allowance simulation, etc.).  
2. Re‑assign each low‑level goal to the correct high‑level goal.  
3. Add missing low‑level goals for the functionalities listed above.  
4. Remove any duplicated or irrelevant goals and ensure each low‑level goal describes a single functional action of the applicant.

[Applicant -> Monitor Application Status] The low‑level goals contain several serious issues. First, they reference many high‑level goals (e.g., Create Application, Manage Application Data, Handle Payments, Submit Application, Simulate Allowance, Provide Informational Services, Collaborate on Application) that are not present in the high‑level goal list, creating a mismatch between the two layers. Second, the actor model is incomplete: the low‑level goals introduce a “Co‑Applicant/Other Parent” actor, yet the actors section defines only a single “Applicant” actor, leading to an inconsistency. Third, while most goals are functional, some are redundant or overly granular (e.g., separate goals for “RetrieveSubmittedApplicationsSummary” and “GetApplicationCurrentStatus” could be merged). Finally, the low‑level goal set does not fully cover all functional aspects described (e.g., real‑time fiscal‑code validation during child addition, draft‑resume options, notification of status changes) in a clear one‑action‑per‑goal format. Overall, the low‑level goals are inconsistent with the defined high‑level goals and actor model, and they miss alignment with the system description.

[Applicant -> Respond to Documentation Requests] The low‑level goals are all functional and each maps to a concrete action an Applicant can perform to satisfy the high‑level goal “Respond to Documentation Requests”. They cover retrieving suspended applications, getting details, uploading required documents, updating requested data fields, and resubmitting the application for review. No non‑functional or unrelated goals are present, and there are no contradictions with the description. The set could be slightly enriched by adding a goal to view the updated status or confirmation after resubmission, but overall the coverage is solid.

[Applicant -> Modify Existing Application] The low‑level goals are largely functional and map well to single actions an applicant can perform when modifying an existing AUU application. They cover selecting an application, retrieving details, adding/updating child data, validating fiscal codes, handling payment information for both parents, adjusting allowance distribution, uploading required documents, confirming suspension requirements, reviewing validation errors, re‑accepting declarations, saving/discarding drafts, reviewing a summary, submitting the modification and downloading a receipt.  

Minor issues:  
1. There is no explicit “Resume Draft” goal (e.g., load a saved draft for continuation), which is a distinct user action described in the system.  
2. A “Delete Child” action is not represented, though the description does not explicitly require it, it could be considered for completeness.  

Adding a low‑level goal such as “ResumeDraftApplication” would improve coverage.

[Applicant -> Access Benefit Information] The low‑level goals only address the “Access Benefit Information” high‑level goal (overview, eligibility criteria, simulation input and result). They completely ignore the core functional capabilities described in the system description, such as creating, saving, and submitting AUU applications; real‑time fiscal‑code validation; handling ISEE data; selecting and providing payment information; accepting declarations and privacy notices; generating receipts; managing drafts; supporting multi‑parent collaboration; adding children to an existing application; uploading supporting documents for suspended applications; and consulting previously submitted applications. Because the low‑level goals are far from comprehensive and omit essential user actions, the set is not representative of the software system.

[Applicant -> Accept Legal Declarations] The low‑level goal set is inconsistent with the high‑level model and the system description.  
* Only one high‑level goal (“Accept Legal Declarations”) is defined, yet the low‑level goals reference many other high‑level goals (e.g., Manage Child Information, Select Payment Method, Upload Supporting Documents, Review and Submit Application, Consult Past Applications, Run Allowance Simulations) that are missing from the high‑level list. This breaks the GORE traceability rule that each low‑level goal must be associated with an existing high‑level goal.  
* Several essential functional actions described in the specification are absent:  
  - Real‑time blocking of a child’s fiscal code when it is already linked to another active application (including duplicate adult‑child checks).  
  - Automatic recalculation of the allowance when a valid ISEE becomes available after submission.  
  - Notification of the applicant about the outcome of the evaluation (accepted, rejected, suspended).  
  - Download of the submission receipt.  
  - Ability for the other parent to complete or modify an already‑submitted application, including changing the allowance distribution and providing their own payment details.  
  - Uploading additional documents after a suspension and reconfirming the application.  
  - Access to general information about the AUU benefit.  
* Some low‑level goals are overly granular or duplicate functionality (e.g., separate “Retrieve” and “Display” actions for declarations) and could be merged for clarity.  
* All goals are functional, but the set is incomplete and misaligned with the defined high‑level goals.

To improve:  
1. Define the missing high‑level goals that reflect the major business objectives (e.g., “Manage Child Information”, “Select Payment Method”, “Submit Application”, “Handle Application Outcomes”, “Support Multi‑Parent Collaboration”, “Automatic Allowance Recalculation”, “Provide Benefit Information”).  
2. Align every low‑level goal with one of these high‑level goals.  
3. Add low‑level goals for the omitted functional actions listed above.  
4. Consolidate overly fine‑grained goals where appropriate.

[Applicant -> Receive Application Receipt] The low‑level goals focus exclusively on receipt handling and many of them describe system‑side behavior (e.g., “Generate Application Receipt”, “Store Application Receipt”, “Display Receipt Availability”) rather than a single action performed by the applicant. According to the GORE rules each low‑level goal should map to an actor’s concrete interaction with the software. Moreover, the only high‑level goal present is “Receive Application Receipt”, which ignores the majority of the functional scope described (application submission, draft saving, child addition, real‑time fiscal‑code validation, ISEE handling, payment method entry, declaration acceptance, document upload for suspended applications, multi‑parent collaboration, status consultation, simulation, etc.). Consequently, the low‑level goal set is both incomplete and mis‑aligned with the actors and the system description.

[Applicant -> Be Informed of Application Outcome] The three low‑level goals are all functional and directly support the single high‑level goal “Be Informed of Application Outcome.” They each describe a distinct interaction (querying status, receiving a status‑change alert, and reviewing past notifications). The only minor issue is that “ReceiveAutomatedStatusChangeNotification” describes a system‑initiated behavior rather than an explicit applicant action; phrasing it as “The applicant shall be able to receive …” would better align with the guideline that each goal corresponds to an actor’s action. Otherwise, the set is consistent and free of non‑functional or irrelevant items.

[Applicant -> Ensure Valid Child Data Submission] The low‑level goal set is poorly aligned with the sole high‑level goal (“Ensure Valid Child Data Submission”). While the first few goals correctly address fiscal‑code format, intra‑application uniqueness, global uniqueness, external data retrieval, storage, and feedback, the majority of the listed goals (draft handling, payment method selection, declaration acceptance, receipt generation, document upload, parent invitation, adding dependents, retrieving past applications, allowance simulation) address completely different concerns that are not covered by any high‑level goal. This violates the GORE principle that each low‑level goal should trace to a specific high‑level objective. Moreover, important functional actions described in the system narrative are missing, such as: real‑time blocking of the flow when a child is already linked to another active application, detection of duplicate adult‑dependent fiscal codes, automatic ISEE‑based allowance recalculation, selection and confirmation of allowance distribution between parents, ability to discard a draft and restart, presentation of a summary screen before submission, and notification of the application outcome. The current list also mixes many API‑centric implementations, which is acceptable, but the lack of correspondence to the defined high‑level goal and the omission of several key applicant actions reduce completeness and consistency.

[Applicant -> Consult Past Applications and History] The low‑level goals correctly map to the single high‑level goal and describe concrete functional actions the applicant can perform (listing applications, viewing details, seeing status history, filtering). They are all functional and pertain to the applicant actor. However, the set is somewhat incomplete: the description also mentions that applicants can download a receipt, view attached documents, and see payment information for past applications. Including low‑level goals such as “The system shall allow the applicant to download the receipt PDF for a submitted application” and “The system shall display any documents attached to a past application” would make the coverage more complete. Adding these would fully represent the functionality described.

[Other Parent -> Complete Shared Application] The low‑level goals are all functional and map clearly to actions that the “Other Parent” actor would perform when completing a shared AUU application. They cover retrieving the application, reviewing entered data, adjusting allowance distribution, providing payment details, accepting declarations, reviewing a summary, submitting, downloading the receipt, and checking status. The set is largely complete and consistent with the description. Minor issues are the slight redundancy between “Retrieve Shared Application Details” and “Display Initiated Application Data” (these could be merged into a single “View Application Details” action) and the absence of an explicit goal for uploading additional documents if the application is suspended (which may be required for the other parent). Addressing these would make the list fully comprehensive.

[Other Parent -> Manage Shared AUU Allowance Distribution and Payment] The low‑level goals are all functional and each maps to a single action that the “Other Parent” can perform on the system (viewing the proposed distribution, confirming it, modifying it, submitting the modification, entering payment details, and submitting those details). They are consistent with the associated high‑level goal and do not contain non‑functional requirements. The set is complete for the scoped high‑level goal, though a brief “Validate entered payment information” step could be added for completeness.

[INPS Staff -> Process and Decide on AUU Applications] The low‑level goals only cover actions performed by INPS staff (retrieving applications, viewing details, handling documents, adding notes, changing status, requesting docs, sending notifications). While these are functional and correctly mapped to the staff actor, they omit all functional goals for the primary users – the applicants/parents – who, according to the description, must be able to start, save, resume, and submit applications; enter child and family data; receive real‑time fiscal‑code validation; select payment methods; accept declarations and privacy notices; upload additional documents; add new children to an existing application; and consult past applications or simulate allowances. Because the low‑level goal set is not a complete representation of the system’s functionality, the model is significantly incomplete.

[INPS Staff -> Automatically Adjust Allowance Based on ISEE] The low‑level goal set is inconsistent with the provided high‑level goals and actors. Only one high‑level goal (automatic ISEE‑based allowance adjustment) is defined, yet the low‑level list contains many applicant‑centric actions (initiate application, save draft, add child, upload documents, confirm declarations, select payment method, submit, retrieve status, view adjustment details, update contact) that belong to a different high‑level goal (“Manage AUU Application and Personal Data”) which is missing from the high‑level specification. This mismatch violates the requirement that each low‑level goal map to a defined high‑level goal.

Furthermore, several low‑level goals are non‑functional or overly administrative (e.g., “Review Allowance Calculation Rules”, “Verify Applicant Notification Content”, “View Allowance Adjustment Audit Log”) and do not represent a single functional action performed by an actor. Important functional actions described in the system description are absent, such as:
- Real‑time fiscal‑code validation and duplicate detection.
- Blocking the flow when a child is already linked to another active application.
- Handling draft discard vs. resume.
- Supporting the other parent’s completion of an application and allowance distribution changes.
- Adding new children to an existing submitted application.
- Simulating allowance amounts and consulting general information.

To improve the model, add the missing high‑level goals (e.g., “Manage AUU Application Lifecycle”, “Support Multi‑Parent Collaboration”, “Provide Information and Simulation Services”) and ensure every low‑level goal is a functional, single‑step action tied to one of those goals. Remove non‑functional review or audit goals, and include the omitted functional actions listed above.

[INPS Staff -> Ensure Timely Allowance Disbursement] The low‑level goal set mixes system‑internal processes (e.g., “Identify Eligible Applications for Monthly Disbursement”, “Initiate Allowance Payment Transaction”, “Record Monthly Disbursement Status”) with actor‑centric actions, violating the rule that each low‑level goal should correspond to a single action performed by an actor through the software. Moreover, many goals are linked to high‑level goals that are not defined in the provided high‑level list (e.g., “Enable Applicants to Submit Complete AUU Applications”, “Support Application Evaluation and Decision”), creating inconsistency. Several essential applicant actions described in the specification are missing (e.g., viewing validation errors, downloading the receipt, cancelling or deleting a draft, confirming the final submission, reviewing the payment schedule). Some goals overlap or are too granular (e.g., separate “Select Payment Method” and “Confirm Payment Method”). To improve the model, restrict low‑level goals to functional, actor‑driven actions, ensure each is tied to an existing high‑level goal, add the missing applicant actions, and remove or re‑classify internal system tasks as non‑functional or separate technical requirements.
